newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN STRIKE RECEIVES TOKEN SUPPORT.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN STRIKE RECEIVES TOKEN SUPPORT.

text.p: A one-day strike called by Bulgaria's biggest trade union on Wednesday to demand a cabinet reshuffle and early parliamentary elections received only token support, witnesses said.
Offices and public transport in the capital Sofia worked normally and the port city of Varna was not affected.
The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions (CITU) said the strike was most effective in the towns of Pleven, Plovdiv and Stara Zagora.
CITU said teachers at more than 300 schools and kindergartens stopped work for an hour, and a spokesman for Plovdiv city transport said its staff had stopped work between 7 a.m. and 8 a.m.
CITU deputy chairman Ivan Neikov said some 477,000 workers in 1,408 firms had joined the protest. By law, health workers, telecommunications staff, the army and the police are forbidden to strike.
"The turnout is good considering the fear and poverty among Bulgarian workers," CITU leader Krastyo Petkov told Reuters.
Some workers staged brief token strikes or wore symbolic protest ribbons.
"There is no strike in the coal mining sector," Energy Minister Roumen Ovcharov told reporters.
The Podkrepa trade union, Bulgaria's second biggest, which is allied with the anti-communist opposition, is not taking part in the protest.
A union statement said it shared CITU's aim of toppling Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov but believed strikes could not resolve the current economic crisis.
The 24 Hours daily said the strike would fail because Petkov's image as a trade union leader was tarnished by his political and business ambitions.
The opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) is not explicitly supporting the strike.
Severe economic crisis has increased pressure on the governing Socialists, whose candidate suffered a decisive defeat in presidential elections last month.

The UDF has called for early elections and says it will not support a currency board regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund to stabilise the economy if it is implemented by the present government.
The currency board, a form of fixed exchange rate regime likely to be introduced early next year, will strengthen Videnov's position if he is seen as bringing back stability.
